passage: It was 7 pm, the office AC had switched off, and Tejas had his own client deck due by midnight. He'd already spent an hour helping the new intern, Rhea, untangle a spreadsheet, and hadn't minded; she'd been stuck, and she'd asked properly. Then Hrithik rolled his chair over. "Bro, can you just finish my summary slide? You're faster." It was the fourth time this month. Tejas remembered the Saturday he'd covered Hrithik's client call, and the cab fare Hrithik had never mentioned again. His stomach tightened; he hated saying no. He took a breath. "Not tonight, and honestly, not like this any more. I'm happy to help when you're stuck. But I've been doing your parts regularly, and it isn't working for me." Hrithik stared, then rolled back. Tejas opened his deck. His hands were a little shaky, and steady enough.

passage: Gurleen's scooter keys hung by the door of her Chandigarh flat, and half the building knew it. She'd picked up Mrs Bedi's medicines from the chemist twice this week without being asked, and lent the scooter to the watchman's son for his college interview. She never kept track. Except with Nilesh from the second floor. He'd borrowed it nine times since Diwali, and it always came back on empty, once with a new scratch nobody explained. On Saturday he knocked again. "Keys, na? Just for an hour." Gurleen kept her hand on the door. "Nilesh, I'm going to stop lending you the scooter. It keeps coming back empty and you never mention it. I'm not angry. I'm just done." He laughed awkwardly. "Over petrol?" "Over the pattern," she said calmly, and closed the door gently.

passage: I'm Yusuf, and I'm the friend with the camera. passage:
Vice-principal's note, 3 March. Written by Mrs Rao.

Sudha, twenty-five, is one of our most generous teachers. She covers classes for anyone who is ill, lends her lesson plans to new staff, and never asks for anything back. This term, though, she has covered Shreya's Class 7 periods eleven times, always at short notice, and Shreya has never once covered for her. Today I overheard Sudha in the staffroom. Shreya asked her to take Friday's periods again. Sudha said, quietly and kindly, "Shreya, I've been happy to help. But it's become every week, and it only goes one way. I can't take Friday." Shreya looked startled. Sudha went back to her marking, hands steady.

What I did next: I checked the cover register and set up a fair rota so cover is shared evenly across the staff.

qa.q: How many times had Sudha covered Shreya's periods this term?
qa.a: She had covered them eleven times.

qa.q: What does Sudha's steady hands after refusing suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and sure about the limit, even though saying no to a colleague was not easy.

qa.q: What did Sudha get right in how she refused?
qa.a: She acknowledged she had been glad to help, named the one-way pattern plainly and kindly, and said no to Friday without blaming Shreya.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel about the new cover rota?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed at first but will know exactly what is expected, and the rest of the staff may feel the system is fairer.

grounding: A generous young teacher who helps freely calmly stops covering for a colleague who only takes, and a fair rota follows.

passage:
Thursday
Covered Elizabeth's shift again today. That's the fourth time this month. She always has a reason: her cousin's wedding, a headache, a friend's party. And she never covers for anyone. When I asked her to swap Saturday, she said she "couldn't possibly."
I don't mind helping. I covered Ravi when his baby was born and I'd do it again. I helped the new girl with the billing system for a week and never expected anything. But Elizabeth takes and takes.
So today I told her, calmly, in the break room: "I've been happy to help. But I can't cover your shifts anymore unless you're able to cover mine sometimes." She looked shocked. I felt my heart pounding, but I didn't take it back. It felt fair.
- Ayesha

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel while telling Elizabeth the limit?
qa.a: Ayesha felt nervous, heart pounding, but steady and sure it was fair.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's approach show about healthy reciprocity?
qa.a: Ayesha stays generous with people who need help but calmly sets a limit with someone who habitually takes.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt hearing Ayesha's limit?
qa.a: Elizabeth looked shocked, perhaps surprised that someone finally named the pattern.

passage: In their village near Nashik, Arohi, twenty-five, kept a small shed of farm tools her late father had left. She lent them to anyone who asked: the widow next door, the schoolteacher, the boys fixing the temple roof. She never kept count. But Gautam, from the upper fields, was different. He borrowed the plough every season, returned it caked in mud, once with a cracked handle, and never lent her his tractor when she asked. This year he came again. Arohi's heart beat faster, but she kept her voice calm. "Gautam-bhai, I've lent you the plough six seasons. When I needed the tractor, you said no. I can't lend it again unless things go both ways." He looked annoyed. "It's just a plough." "Then you won't miss it," she said, and closed the shed door gently.

In the Buenos Aires office, Mateo was known for helping. He covered Saturday shifts, lent his charger and never kept count.
Beatriz, a colleague, asked him to finish her reports four Fridays in a row so she could leave early. She never asked what he needed. When his mother was ill, he asked her to cover one Monday. She said she couldn't.
The next Friday, she came to his desk. "Mateo, could you do my report again?"
He looked up calmly. "No, Beatriz. I've helped you a lot, and I'm happy to help when it's a real crunch. But I can't keep doing your reports while you leave early."
She blinked. "Oh. Okay."
He went back to helping the new intern with a spreadsheet.

At the district hospital, Kashish was the junior doctor who always said yes. She swapped night shifts, stayed late to help new interns, and covered for friends with sick children.
Jagdish asked her to swap shifts nine times in two months. He never swapped back. When she needed Diwali evening off, he said, "Sorry, I have plans."
The next week he asked again. "Kashish, one more swap? Saturday night?"
She took a breath. "Jagdish, I've swapped nine times and you haven't swapped once. I'm happy to help in emergencies. But I'm not doing Saturday."
He muttered and walked away.
That evening she stayed an extra hour to help an intern who was struggling. Helping still felt good.

qa.a: She likely felt nervous but determined, ready to set a limit after being taken for granted.

I've really liked sharing the flat with you this year. I've lent you money for rent twice, driven you to the station at five in the morning, and cooked for you when you were ill. I was glad to. I don't keep count.

Yash

passage: Kavitha, you'll be asked for favours all the time here, so let me tell you about my first job. I was twenty-four, a skinny boy called Sumit from Nagpur with a good head for spreadsheets. I helped everyone: fixed formulas, stayed late to check reports, never kept count. Most people helped back one day or another; Farooq brought me biryani the night my father was in hospital. But one colleague, Rakesh, came every Friday at six with "just one small thing", and it was always his whole report. For months I said yes. Then one Friday I heard him tell the boss he had "worked all night" on it. On Monday I told him calmly, "I'll help when you're stuck, Rakesh. I won't do your work any more." He sulked for a week. I kept helping everyone else, just as before. Generous doesn't mean blind, Kavitha.
